analysis.one_liner: Repeals the annual fee that the Affordable Care Act charges health insurance companies.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 231 cosponsors but never received a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Care Act charges health insurers an annual fee, paid starting in 2014, that helps fund the law's coverage programs. This bill would erase that fee entirely, removing a multi-billion-dollar-a-year charge on the insurance industry. The bill never got a vote in committee and died at the end of the 113th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurance companies would gain the most: they would no longer pay the annual fee the ACA imposes on them. Supporters, including some Democrats, argued the fee is passed on to customers in the form of higher premiums, so anyone buying coverage could see some benefit if repeal lowered premiums. The federal government would collect less revenue, which under the ACA helps fund premium tax credits and coverage expansions.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the annual fee on health insurance providers enacted by the Affordable Care Act by striking section 9010 of the law.
The CRS summary confirms the bill would eliminate the annual fee on health insurance providers that was set to begin in 2014 under the ACA.
Supporters of repealing the insurer fee generally argued the fee is passed through to consumers in higher premiums, so repeal would ease premium pressure on people buying coverage.
The bill attracted broad support in the House, with 231 cosponsors, including 222 Republicans and 9 Democrats, showing substantial appetite for the repeal among House members.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would lose the revenue from the fee, which under the ACA helps pay for premium subsidies and coverage programs. That lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers, by larger deficits, or by smaller health coverage benefits. The fee is levied on insurers in proportion to their premiums, so the largest, most profitable insurers pay the most.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the fee removes revenue the ACA relies on to help finance its premium tax credits and coverage expansions, so the cost of the law would shift to other taxpayers or the deficit.

The fee falls on insurers in proportion to their premiums, so repeal is a direct, permanent tax cut for the health insurance industry, which would keep the benefit regardless of whether insurers actually reduce premiums for customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If repeal lowered premiums, customers buying coverage would benefit somewhat, but the main and certain beneficiary is the insurance industry, which would stop paying a multi-billion-dollar annual fee. The offsetting cost is real: the fee is one of the ACA's dedicated funding streams, so repealing it either deepens deficits or forces cuts or tax increases elsewhere to preserve coverage subsidies. The bill offered no replacement revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees for the rest of the 113th Congress and never received a vote in either committee or on the floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 15, 2013 by Rep. Charles Boustany with bipartisan original cosponsors and was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee.
It gathered 231 cosponsors, including 222 Republicans and 9 Democrats, making it one of the more broadly supported ACA-related repeal bills in the House.
In April 2013, at a member's request, the bill was re-referred so that Ways and Means became the primary committee, but no committee considered it.
The bill never advanced out of committee and received no vote in the House or Senate before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, health insurers continue paying the annual ACA fee, and the federal revenue that helps fund the law's coverage subsidies was preserved. The public interest in keeping that funding stream was better off than it would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The ACA's funding stream survived; insurers keep paying

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican — 222 of 233 House Republicans cosponsored — with only 9 Democrats joining, and the bill never advanced in a House fully controlled by the sponsor's own party.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently removed the ACA's annual fee, a multi-billion-dollar yearly charge on insurers proportional to their premiums. Insurers argued the fee raises premiums, so their interest in repeal partly overlaps with customers', but the fee also funds the ACA's coverage programs, so repeal would shift that cost to other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Federal health coverage programs (premium tax credits)
industries.note: The fee is one of the ACA's dedicated funding sources for premium subsidies and coverage expansions. Repealing it would cut that funding, raising costs for other taxpayers or reducing support for people buying coverage.
